This makes it easier for developers to build applications that take advantage of the security features provided by the Hyper Protect Crypto Services cloud HSM.

The Keep Your Own Key (KYOK) feature in Hyper Protect Crypto Services enables users to configure the master key to take full control of the cloud Hardware Security Module (HSM), ensuring that only they have access to their encryption keys. This feature is enabled by configuring the master key, which allows users to have full control and authority over the encryption keys they bring, control, and manage. No one except the user has access to their encryption keys, providing a high level of security and control.

Yes, Hyper Protect Crypto Services can be used for data-at-rest encryption with customer-owned keys in integration with other IBM Cloud data and storage services. The service provides seamless integration with other IBM Cloud data and storage services, enabling users to create, import, rotate, and manage keys with the standardized API. Once the encryption keys are deleted, users can be assured that their data that is protected by these keys is no longer retrievable. The service is built on FIPS 140-2 Level 4 certified HSM, offering the highest level of protection in the cloud industry.

Unified Key Orchestrator provides a single point-of-control of encryption keys across hybrid multicloud environments, including on-premises environments. When used with Hyper Protect Crypto Services, Unified Key Orchestrator enables users with both Keep Your Own Key and Bring Your Own Key capabilities across their hybrid multicloud environments. Unified Key Orchestrator manages and orchestrates all keys from the multicloud environments on IBM Cloud.

Hyper Protect Crypto Services supports the use of encryption keys for data protection in internet repositories and services such as anti-virus virus definitions and two-factor authentication servers. This ensures that data remains secure even when it is stored in these repositories or transmitted over public networks.

Yes, Hyper Protect Crypto Services supports cloud-based cryptographic operations, including data-at-rest encryption with customer-owned keys and PKCS #11 cryptography. It enables users to perform cryptographic operations with the highest level of security and efficiency, on FIPS 140-2 Level 4-certified hardware.

Yes, the IBM Watson Speech to Text service can transcribe numbers as digits instead of strings for US English, Japanese, and Spanish audio using smart formatting. This feature is currently in beta. Smart formatting can also convert certain strings such as times, phone numbers, and currency symbols into conventional representations.

Smart formatting is a beta feature that converts certain strings such as dates, times, series of digits and numbers, phone numbers, currency values (for US English and Spanish), and internet email and web addresses (for US English and Spanish) into more conventional representations. You can enable smart formatting by setting the smart\_formatting parameter to true. The service applies smart formatting just before it returns the final results to the client, when text normalization is complete. This conversion makes the transcript more readable and promotes better post-processing of transcription results by representing these artifacts as they would normally be written. Smart formatting affects only words in the transcript field of final results, those results for which the final field is true. It does not affect interim results, for which final is false. It also does not affect words in other fields of the response. Smart formatting does not affect previous-generation models which produce hesitation markers to replace hesitations in a transcript, however for US English, smart formatting suppresses hesitation markers from the transcript field for final results.

Smart formatting converts the following types of strings into more conventional representations: dates, times, series of digits and numbers, phone numbers, currency values (for US English and Spanish), and internet email and web addresses (for US English and Spanish). For more information about the specific strings that trigger smart formatting changes, see the following sections: * [Smart formatting for US English and Spanish](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/speech-to-text?topic=speech-to-text-formattingsmart-formatting-english-spanish) * [Smart formatting for Japanese](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/speech-to-text?topic=speech-to-text-formattingsmart-formatting-japanese)

To enable smart formatting, you can set the smart_formatting parameter to true. Smart formatting is beta functionality and is available for US English, Japanese, and Spanish (all dialects). It is also available for the en-WW_Medical_Telephony model when US English audio is recognized. By default, the service does not perform smart formatting. The service applies smart formatting just before it returns the final results to the client, when text normalization is complete.
No, smart formatting only affects words in the transcript field of final results, those results for which the final field is true. It does not affect interim results, for which final is false.

For US English, smart formatting suppresses hesitation markers from the transcript field for final results. Hesitation markers, such as "uhm" and "uh", can adversely impact the conversion of phrases and strings by smart formatting for some languages.

If you set the redaction parameter to true, the service automatically forces the smart_formatting parameter to be true, and it disables the keywords, keywords_threshold, max_alternatives, and (for the WebSocket interface) interim_results parameters. The redaction parameter is an optional boolean that allows the service to automatically redact sensitive numeric information from a final transcript. This parameter is beta functionality and is restricted to certain languages.

Intel® Software Guard Extension (SGX) is an architecture extension designed to enhance security by using protected memory areas for sensitive code and data. To provision a bare metal server with SGX: (1) Create a custom server by following the relevant procedure, then (2) on the bare metal provisioning page, select a single processor Intel Xeon® 2174 with storage up to four drives and an appropriate image such as Windows 2019 or Linux 16.04 LTS. On the order form, choose the Software Guard Extensions (SGX) add-on. Lastly, install Intel SGX platform software and drivers from the Intel open source website.

Intel SGX supports several operating systems, including Windows Server 2019, Windows Server 2016 Standard Edition (64 bit), Windows Server 2016 Datacenter Edition (64 bit), CentOS 7.x (64 bit), Ubuntu Linux 16.04 LTS Xenial Xerus (64 bit), CentOS 8.x (64 bit), and RHEL® 8.x (64 bit) (per-processor licensing).

In an SGX environment, the attestation process ensures that information is kept confidential and data leakage is prevented. At runtime, segmented information is kept confidential through attestation. When a request for information from the segmented code or app data is received, the enclave verifies that the request comes from the part of the application that exists outside of the enclave within the same application before sharing any information. Through this process, information is kept confidential and data leakage is prevented.
No, to work with Intel SGX, you must use specific machine types, such as me4c.4x32 and me4c.4x32.1.9tb.ssd. These machine types are designed to support the installation and operation of Intel SGX.

The specific instructions for installing Intel SGX on Linux can be found in the [Intel SGX Installation Guide for Linux](https://download.01.org/intel-sgx/linux-2.1.2/docs/Intel_SGX_Installation_Guide_Linux_2.1.2_Open_Source.pdf).

Spare pools in the IBM Cloud are a feature that allows users to manage the spare pool of devices associated with their account. Each device in the spare pool can be used as a backup device if more devices are needed. The spare pools feature is accessible through the Spare Pool screen in the IBM Cloud.
Yes, you can now order extra block and file storage (20 - 12,000 GB) when you provision a bare metal server on the IBM Cloud.

Smart Routing improves network performance by analyzing and optimizing routing decisions across the internet using real-time network connections. It reduces latency on average by 35% and connection errors by 27%, by efficiently routing connections and avoiding packet loss, congestion, and outages. Tiered Caching, on the other hand, increases cache hit ratios using concentrated connections to reduce requests to customer origins. It decreases the load on the origin server by taking advantage of cached data and concentrating connections to origin servers. When used together, Smart Routing and Tiered Caching optimize paths for data transmission and reduce the distance data travels, further minimizing latency and improving network performance.

The `ibmcloud cis routing-update` command allows you to modify the routing settings for a DNS domain. There are several command options available for this command. The required option is the `DNS_DOMAIN_ID`, which is the ID of the DNS domain that you want to modify. Other options include:

* `--smart-routing`: This option enables or disables Smart Routing. You can use either the `on` or `off` values.
* `--tiered-caching`: This option enables or disables Tiered Caching. You can use either the `on` or `off` values.
* `-i, --instance`: This option specifies the instance name or ID. If not set, the context instance specified by `ibmcloud cis instance-set INSTANCE` is used.
* `--output`: This option specifies the output format. Only JSON format is supported.

Here's an example command that modifies the routing settings for a domain:
```sh
ibmcloud cis routing-update 31984fea73a15b45779fa0df4ef62f9b --smart-routing on --tiered-caching on -i "cis-demo"
```
This command modifies the routing settings for the domain with the ID `31984fea73a15b45779fa0df4ef62f9b`, and enables both Smart Routing and Tiered Caching for the `"cis-demo"` instance. The output format is JSON.

Yes, you can manually purge files from the cache.  Cached files have a specified expiration time, known as the Time-to-live (TTL) after which they are purged from the cache. If you want to remove a file from the cache immediately, you can manually purge it from the CIS cache.  To manually purge a file from the cache, you can use the `ibmcloud cis cache-purge` command. You will need to provide the URL of the file that you want to purge. Once the command is executed, the file will be removed from the CIS cache immediately.  Keep in mind that purging a file from the cache means that the file will be removed from all CIS data centers across the globe, not just from a single data center. However, please note that the next request for the file will still result in a cache miss, and the file will need to be fetched from the origin server again to be cached at the data center.

The default caching behavior of Cloud Internet Services (CIS) caches static content depending on where your visitors come from, which CIS data center your visitors reach, and how often visitors request a resource at the specific data center. CIS only caches a resource within the CIS data center that serves the request and doesn’t cache off-site or third-party resources, such as those from social networking sites (e.g., Facebook, Flickr). Additionally, it does not cache content hosted on unproxied DNS records. By default, CIS respects the origin web server’s cache headers unless overridden by an edge cache TTL page rule.

If you enable Smart Routing for your domain, Cloud Internet Services (CIS) will begin using real-time network intelligence to route traffic across paths from the origin to a CIS data center. This can help eliminate excess latency, reduce internet latency on average by 35%, and connection errors by 27%.  The optimized route is different from the regular request path. It can take up to 24 hours for CIS to switch from the regular request path to the optimized route after enabling Smart Routing for your domain.  It's worth noting that Smart Routing is a paid feature available only with Enterprise plans. You can enable or disable it using the `ibmcloud cis routing-update` command with the `--smart-routing on` or `--smart-routing off` options, respectively.

Tiered Caching reduces requests to customer origins by first asking other Points of Presence (PoPs) if they have the requested data when a cache miss takes place.  Instead of going back to the origin server to retrieve the requested data, Tiered Caching will first check if any of the other PoPs have the data in their cache. If any of the PoPs have the data in their cache, Tiered Caching will serve the data from the nearest possible location, hence reducing the requests to customer origins.  This way, customers see a performance increase because distances between the PoPs are typically shorter than the distances between PoPs and origins. By taking advantage of the cached data, customers benefit from a decrease in the load on their origin server. Tiered Caching also concentrates connections to origin servers so they come from a smaller number of PoPs, allowing fewer open connections going to the origin.

The impact of purging files from the cache manually is that CIS goes back to your origin server to reload your files and update the cache with the latest versions. This can result in a faster response time when serving those files to customers, as they will be served from the nearest possible location. However, purging files from the cache manually can also result in temporarily higher load on your origin server.

Time-to-live (TTL) is the length of time that a file remains in the cache before it is purged. By default, CIS uses the origin web server’s cache headers to determine the TTL for each file, but this can be overridden by setting an edge cache TTL page rule.  The TTL is important because it helps to keep the cache fresh and up-to-date. A longer TTL means that files will stay in the cache longer, reducing the need to request them from the origin server. This can help to improve load times and decrease server load. But if the files change often, a longer TTL may mean that users receive outdated information.  On the other hand, a shorter TTL means that files are cached for a shorter period of time, which can be helpful if the files are updated frequently. However, this may increase server load and decrease load times.  The ideal TTL will depend on the specific use case and requirements of your application or website.

When federating identities with your IBM Cloud account, there are two options: IBMid and IBM Cloud App ID. IBMid is a global service that allows you to federate to your own corporate user directory or a third-party Identity Provider (IdP) service, simplifying the process of adding users to your account without requiring a separate password. However, for cases where using IBMid to federate your corporate user directory is not feasible, IBM Cloud App ID can be created in your account and connected to your chosen IdP. Both methods support SAML federation, but IBM Cloud App ID allows for advanced functionality such as resetting passwords directly in your app.

Yes, you can use your IBMid to access all IBM Cloud resources. IBMid is the user identity and access management service for IBM web-based services, including IBM Cloud. You can use your IBMid to log in to IBM Cloud, as well as other IBM web offerings. Additionally, when you federate with IBMid, you can use your company's email address and password to access IBM Cloud resources. This simplifies the process of adding users to your account, without requiring an IBMid with a separate password. However, there may be cases where it is not feasible to use IBMid to federate your corporate user directory, in which case you can create an IBM Cloud App ID instance in your account and connect it to your chosen IdP.

Federated IBMid users are users who connect their internal user directory, or IdP, with IBMid so that they don't need to manage an additional password. They can reuse their normal login to their IdP to log in to IBM web offerings, including IBM Cloud. Connecting an external IdP with IBMid is called federation, and the technical underlying protocol is called SAML.
On the other hand, IBM Cloud App ID users are users who are authenticated using IBM Cloud App ID service, which can connect to only one external IdP using SAML, so a unique email address is not required. IBM Cloud App ID is a user identity and access management service specifically designed for mobile and web applications. It allows you to configure one or several identity providers to create a custom sign-in experience for your users.

To create an IBM Cloud account, you need an IBMid user that will be the IBM Cloud account owner. You can create this IBMid user during the IBM Cloud account registration process or use an existing IBMid user. We recommend creating the account by using a functional ID or service account with a valid email address to simplify account ownership continuity in your organization. For any additional members of your IBM Cloud account, you have the option to use normal or federated IBMid users as IBM Cloud account members. Alternatively, you can connect your IdP to your IBM Cloud account by using an IBM Cloud App ID service instance. All users that log in through that IBM Cloud App ID service instance are added to your account automatically, so you don't need to invite those users.

IBMid is IBM's IDaaS used to access IBM Cloud resources and can be federated with a user's own corporate directory or third-party IdP services like Okta. It simplifies the user addition process but may not be feasible for certain use cases. An alternative, IBM Cloud App ID, requires creating an instance in the user's account and connecting it to their chosen IdP. It's a self-service option with a low-usage fee but requires a custom URL to log in to IBM Cloud. IBMid is more suitable when an enterprise wants to connect their internal directory with IBMid, while IBM Cloud App ID is suitable for those who prefer a self-service option and can accommodate the custom URL login.

Federating with IBMid simplifies the process of adding users to an IBM Cloud account by allowing users to reuse their existing login credentials with IBMid. When you federate with IBMid, users don't need to create an IBM Cloud account or manage a separate password for IBM Cloud. Instead, they can use their existing IBMid to log in to IBM Cloud and access its resources. This can save time and reduce the risk of creating weak passwords or forgetting passwords. Federating with IBMid also allows users to access other IBM web offerings by using the same IBMid.

The process of federating with IBMid involves connecting your internal user directory, or IdP, with IBMid so that your employees don't need to manage an additional password. If your company's email domain is already federated with IBMid, you can start configuring access to your account. If your company's email domain is not already federated with IBMid, a manual process with the IBMid federation team is required to establish federation.

Creating an IBM Cloud App ID instance and connecting it to a chosen IdP differs from federating with IBMid in a few ways. First, IBM Cloud App ID allows for a more customizable login experience, as it allows for custom sign-in pages, custom error pages, and custom emails. Additionally, IBM Cloud App ID can connect to only one external IdP using SAML, while IBMid can federate with multiple enterprise customers at the same time. This means that a unique email address isn't required with IBM Cloud App ID, unlike with IBMid where a unique email address for each IBMid user is a prerequisite for successful federation.

Yes, a unique email address is required for each IBMid user when federating with IBMid. This is because IBMid is federating with multiple enterprise customers at the same time, and a successful federation requires a unique identifier for each user. The email address used for the IBMid account is also used as the identifier for the user when federating with IBMid.

Yes, there are limitations when connecting an IdP to an IBM Cloud App ID instance. An App ID instance can connect to only one external IdP using SAML, and therefore a unique email address isn't required. This means that if you need to connect to multiple IdPs, you'll need to create multiple App ID instances. Additionally, there is a low-usage fee associated with creating an App ID instance, and a custom URL is required to log in to IBM Cloud.

Using a functional ID or service account as the IBM Cloud account owner can help simplify account ownership continuity in your organization. This is because functional IDs or service accounts are not tied to a specific individual, making it easier to transfer ownership or manage the account in the event that the original owner leaves the organization. Additionally, using a functional ID or service account can make it easier to manage access controls and permissions within the IBM Cloud account.

When you provision an instance, the total instance bandwidth is allocated between attached volumes and networking. The initial allocation depends on the bandwidth set by an API or the instance profile selected. If not specified, 25% is allocated to volume bandwidth and 75% to network bandwidth. For example, a bx2-2x8 balanced server profile allows a total bandwidth of 4,000 Mbps (4 Gbps), with 1,000 Mbps for volumes and 3,000 Mbps for the network. You can see these allocations via the /instance/profiles API endpoint or during instance creation in the UI. The allocation can be adjusted to balance between network bandwidth and volume bandwidth, but both must be at least 500 Mbps each. Network bandwidth can be automatically adjusted after setting storage bandwidth. You can use the CLI or API to adjust total storage bandwidth, which results in a corresponding decrease in network bandwidth. The minimum network bandwidth is 500 Mbps.

Yes, you can see the bandwidth allocations in the profile information during instance creation in the UI. For example, for the bx2-2x8 profile, you might have:
Volumes: 1,000 Mbps
Network: 3,000 Mbps
This will give you an idea of how the bandwidth is allocated between volumes and networking for the specific instance profile you have selected during instance provisioning.
If the total maximum bandwidth of attached volumes exceeds the amount available on the instance, the bandwidth for each attached volume is set proportionally based on each volume's maximum bandwidth.

To ensure reasonable boot times, a minimum of 393 Mbps of volume bandwidth is allocated to the boot volume. In the example that has the instance's total volume bandwidth of 1,000 Mbps, the remaining 607 Mbps is allocated to any secondary volumes that you attach, up to the maximum bandwidth of the volume. For example, if you have one data volume with 500 Mbps, you can expect to get that level of performance.

No, you cannot adjust the volume bandwidth without changing the network bandwidth. The allocation of the instance's total bandwidth can be adjusted, balancing between network bandwidth and volume bandwidth. To increase the volume bandwidth, you will need to decrease the network bandwidth proportionally.

Before you change the bandwidth ratio, make sure that you evaluate your instance's network bandwidth requirements. Make sure that the new bandwidth allocation does not have negative effects on your instance’s network performance. For example, if you allocate too much bandwidth to secondary volumes and not enough to network, it can negatively affect your instance’s network performance.

Profiles can have a total maximum bandwidth of up to 80 Gbps. That bandwidth is split between Network and Storage traffic. The network bandwidth allocation is distributed evenly across network interfaces, and each network interface has a cap of 25 Gbps. You might need to attach multiple network interfaces to your virtual server instance to optimize network performance. For example, if you choose the bx2-32x128 profile, the total bandwidth that is assigned for the instance is 64 Gbps. The default network cap is 48 Gbps for network and 16 Gbps for storage, but this amount can be adjusted. If you use the default bandwidth allocation and a single network interface on the instance, that vNIC has a port speed of 25 Gbps. If two network interfaces are on the system, each network interface has a port speed of 24 Gbps, for a total aggregate network bandwidth for 48 Gbps.

IBM Cloud offers a combination of platform as a service (PaaS) with infrastructure as a service (IaaS), providing an integrated experience that scales for both small and large enterprises. It ensures high levels of compliance, security, and management with proven architecture patterns and methods for rapid delivery of mission-critical workloads. IBM Cloud offers the most open and secure public cloud for business with a next-generation hybrid cloud platform, advanced data and AI capabilities. Furthermore, IBM Cloud Schematics is a managed Terraform service that allows you to use native Terraform capabilities for predictable and consistent provisioning of IBM Cloud resources.

Terraform is an open-source software that enables predictable and consistent provisioning of IBM Cloud platform, classic infrastructure, and VPC infrastructure resources by using a high-level scripting language. It can be used to create a single or multi-zone Kubernetes and Red Hat OpenShift cluster on IBM Cloud. By using Terraform, users can define their infrastructure as code, which simplifies the process of setting up and managing infrastructure resources. Terraform allows users to manage complex infrastructures with ease and provides features such as version control, testing, and continuous monitoring. Using Terraform with IBM Cloud Schematics, users can skip setting up and maintaining the Terraform CLI and IBM Cloud Provider plug-in, making it easier to manage their infrastructure resources.

When using the Schematics user interface on IBM Cloud, you enter the GitHub repository for SAP S4HANA Schematics, while for the Catalog Tile, you select the SAP S/4HANA tile from the catalog. The Schematics user interface allows you to enter workspace information, modify the parameters in the Schematics interface, and enter the Github path, while the Catalog Tile creates a Schematics workspace for you and enables you to modify the parameters for your bastion server, personal credential information, and other parameters specific to your solution. It is important to note that Schematics and Terraform have no warranties of any kind and no service or technical support available from IBM, while the Catalog Tile offering is IBM Cloud supported.

SAP Kits are archives that contain the necessary SAP and DB kits that need to be downloaded to your Deployment Server. The IBM Cloud platform allocates temporary storage on a dedicated Jump host for each region and it is the responsibility of the user to download the necessary kits. During the automation deployment process, Ansible decompresses the file archives. SAP Kits are used in the deployment process on IBM Cloud to ensure that the necessary software is available for deployment and automation. The use of SAP Kits helps to streamline the deployment process and ensures that the necessary components are in place before beginning the deployment.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the practice of defining and managing your infrastructure using configuration files. This approach enables organizations to treat their infrastructure as code, making it easier to version, manage and maintain. IaC allows you to automate the provisioning and management of infrastructure resources, rather than manually provisioning and configuring them. In the context of IBM Cloud, IaC helps users codify their cloud environment, making it easier to automate the provisioning and management of resources. This leads to improved efficiency, fewer manual errors, and faster time to market. Additionally, IaC makes it simpler to ensure consistency across multiple environments and regions, making it an essential practice in modern cloud computing.

IBM Cloud Schematics Workspaces are provided to you at no cost. However, when you decide to apply your Terraform template in IBM Cloud, you are charged for the IBM Cloud resources that are described in your Terraform template. The charges for these resources depend on the service plans and pricing information for each resource that you are about to create. To manage the charges associated with using IBM Cloud Schematics, you can review available service plans and pricing information for each resource before you apply the Terraform template. Some services come with a limit per IBM Cloud account, so it's important to check the service quota and increase it if necessary, or remove existing services before provisioning new ones. Additionally, IBM Cloud Schematics ibmcloud terraform command usage displays warning and deprecation messages as Alias Terraform are deprecated, which can help you keep track of changes and updates.

IBM Cloud Schematics provides powerful tools to automate cloud infrastructure provisioning and management by using open source projects such as Terraform, Ansible, Red Hat OpenShift, Operators, and Helm, and delivering these capabilities to you as a managed service. Rather than installing each open source project on your system, and learn the API or CLI, you can declare the tasks that you want to run in IBM Cloud and watch Schematics run these tasks for you. This approach enables you to focus on your code and business logic, instead of worrying about the underlying infrastructure. With Schematics, you can ensure consistent and reliable deployments, and reduce the time and effort required to manage and maintain your cloud infrastructure.

To allow users in Microsoft Azure to perform various actions for Satellite, you can grant them the general Contributor built-in role in Azure role-based access control. For more information about further restricting permissions, please refer to the Azure documentation.

To manually create a Satellite location in AWS, the following permissions are required: AmazonEC2FullAccess, AmazonElasticFileSystemFullAccess, AmazonVPCFullAccess, and AWSMarketplaceFullAccess. For further restriction of permissions, consult the AWS documentation.

Yes, if you added more than 6 hosts, the additional hosts are unassigned and available for use in the control plane or by services. If you need OpenShift Data Foundation or similar services, review the required resources and manually create hosts in your Azure account. Then, attach the hosts to your location. Make sure you have the correct IBM Cloud permissions to create locations, including to Satellite and Schematics.

To sign in to your Azure account from the command line, you can use the Azure CLI command "az login". You will need to provide your Azure account credentials to authenticate the login. For more information, see the Azure documentation.

In IBM Cloud Satellite, an app developer requires viewer platform role for the Satellite location and writer or deployer service access role for the configuration resources. They also need editor platform role and writer service role to Red Hat OpenShift clusters or particular projects in a cluster to deploy and manage their applications.

In IBM Cloud Satellite, do not reuse the same name for multiple locations, even after the other location is deleted. If you use the same name 5 times or more within 7 days, you might reach the Let's Encrypt Duplicate Certificate rate limit.

The IBM Cloud IAM API key is used to create the template and manage its resources in IBM Cloud Satellite. Satellite automatically creates an IBM Cloud IAM API key, but you can optionally provide the value of an existing API key that has the correct permissions in the same account.

Backup your Knowledge Studio workspace data by completing the following steps: 1. Understand which data can be backed up. 2. Prepare for backup. 3. Download artifacts from the current instance. To restore the backup, perform the following steps: 1. Re-create workspaces on the new instance. 2. Restore the workspace data. 3. Restore the models. 4. Restore any incomplete annotation tasks. To ensure data integrity during backup or restore, stop Knowledge Studio front-end pods and confirm no training or evaluation processes are running.

Yes, you can backup and restore a single database in your Knowledge Studio instance. However, to ensure that users don't have access to Knowledge Studio while you perform the backup or restore, it's recommended to stop the Knowledge Studio front-end pods before you start the backup or restore process. It's also essential to make sure that no training and evaluation processes are running before you begin the backup or restore process. Once you have completed the backup or restore process, you can reactivate Knowledge Studio using the appropriate command.

The following types of artifacts can be backed up and migrated manually:
1. Editable dictionaries
2. Type system
3. Approved ground truth document sets

To prepare for backing up and restoring your data, you should complete any work that is in progress in your workspace. Specifically, you should finish any in-progress annotation tasks. Only documents that have been annotated, adjudicated, and approved and promoted to ground truth can be backed up. If you do not finish the annotation work, you will lose any annotation effort that is in progress but not completely done. Additionally, you should make a list of any outstanding annotation tasks and document sets that have not been added to the ground truth yet before you back up your data.

If you don't finish the annotation work before backing up, you will lose any annotation effort that is in progress but not completely done. Only documents that have been annotated, adjudicated, and approved and promoted to ground truth can be backed up. If you have any in-progress annotation tasks that you haven't finished, you will not be able to restore them after the backup.

To deploy a container into the default namespace of a cluster, follow these steps:

1. Create an image pull secret: Refer to the IBM documentation for creating an image pull secret. [Using an image pull secret to access images in other IBM Cloud accounts or external private registries from non-default Kubernetes namespaces](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/containers?topic=containers-registryother)

2. Verify that your image pull secret was added to your default service account: Use the command `oc describe serviceaccount default -n <project_name>` to verify if your image pull secret is present.

3. Create a pod configuration file: Use a YAML file, such as mypod.yaml, to deploy a container from an image in your registry. The YAML file should contain the configuration required for your deployment. In this file, specify the correct name and tag of your image in the deployment YAML file: `image: <region>.icr.io/<project>/<image>:<tag>`

4. Create the pod in the cluster: Use the command `oc apply -f mypod.yaml` to apply the mypod.yaml configuration file and create the pod in the cluster.

5. Refer to the image pull secret in your pod deployment: In your pod configuration file, include the `imagePullSecrets` field to reference the image pull secret. The `imagePullSecrets` field contains the name of the image pull secret you created.

For example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mypod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: mypod-container
    image: <region>.icr.io/<project>/<image>:<tag>
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: my-secret-name
```

Replace `my-secret-name` with the name of your image pull secret. In this example, the image pull secret is referenced in the pod deployment using the `name` field within the `imagePullSecrets` field.

The purpose of creating a Kubernetes secret named `hsmcrypto` in the service instance namespace is to provide the necessary keys and configuration files for the HSM client image to be accessed by a CA, peer, or ordering node in the IBM Blockchain Platform. When a node that is configured with HSM is deployed in the console, it uses this secret to access the HSM client image keys and configuration files. This allows for secure communication between the node and the HSM client image.

You can verify the contents of the `hsmcrypto` secret by running the following command:

`kubectl get secret hsmcrypto -n <NAMESPACE> -o yaml`

This will display the contents of the secret in YAML format. Replace `<NAMESPACE>` with the name of your service instance namespace or OpenShift project.

An image pull secret is a Kubernetes secret that contains authentication credentials for accessing container images in a private container registry. In order to deploy containers from a private registry, you must create an image pull secret and add it to your Kubernetes service account.

The potential causes of downtime for IBM Cloud Databases for MySQL include network outages, storage and volume-related issues, high CPU usage, high disk I/O, and connection overloads. Databases for MySQL is designed with a cluster containing three data members: a leader and two replicas. In case the leader becomes unreachable, a controlled switchover or failover occurs, and one of the replicas is promoted to leader. This process maintains data integrity, but temporary connection interruptions can happen during failovers. If both replicas are lost, writes to the leader can hang due to the semisynchronous replication process. In this case, the database might trigger a graceful failover, retry, and reconnect to minimize interruptions. To reduce the risk of interruptions, updates are applied to replicas first and lastly the leader, and failovers generally take less than 30 seconds.

In MySQL, deployments contain a cluster with three data members: a leader and two replicas. In PostgreSQL, deployments contain a cluster with two data members: a leader and a replica. Both members in PostgreSQL contain a copy of the data using asynchronous replication, with a distributed consensus mechanism to maintain the cluster state and handle failovers. This allows for faster and more efficient data replication than MySQL's semi-synchronous replication. Additionally, PostgreSQL allows for the extension of high availability by adding more members for greater in-region redundancy or provisioning read-only replicas for cross-regional failover or read offloading.

IBM Cloud Databases for EnterpriseDB typically contains a cluster with three data members: a leader and two replicas. The replica members contain a copy of your data from the leader using asynchronous replication and a distributed consensus mechanism. This configuration provides more protection against zonal outages and improves the safety of synchronous transactions when compared to MySQL and PostgreSQL, which have fewer data members. In double-entry bookkeeping, debits and credits are used to record financial transactions in a way that allows for accuracy and balance. The purpose of debits and credits is to ensure that every transaction is recorded in two different places, with the total debits equaling the total credits. This balance is what makes the balance sheet balance.

In the context of cooking a simple breakfast, debits and credits can be illustrated using the example of breaking eggs and putting them in a frying pan. When an egg is broken, the asset (the egg) is split into parts, and some of the asset goes into the pan and some into the trash. A debit is used to show that the assets in the pan and the trash both increase, while a balancing credit is used to show that the amount of assets (whole eggs) in the egg carton has decreased. This transaction is in balance because the total credits equal the total debits.

In the context of a bank checking account, debits and credits work as follows: 

When money is deposited into a checking account, it is treated as a credit transaction (increase) because checking account balances are bank liabilities. Conversely, when money is paid out, it is treated as a debit transaction (decrease). 

However, from the bank's perspective, a customer's checking account is a liability, but the cash deposited is a bank asset. So, a cash deposit becomes two equal increases: a debit to cash on hand (bank asset) and a credit to the customer's checking account (bank liability).

In the context of a credit card account, the viewpoint of debits and credits differs between an individual and a bank. To an individual, a credit card is a liability, as they owe the bank money. Therefore, when they post a charge, it is considered a credit (increase in liability), and when they pay it off, it is considered a debit (decrease in liability). However, from the bank's perspective, the individual's credit card account is an asset, as the customer owes them money. So, to the bank, a charge is a debit (increase in asset), and a payment is a credit (decrease in asset). This highlights the importance of perspective in understanding debits and credits.

In the US, stocks are taxed based on the gain or loss realized when you sell the stock. To determine the gain or loss, you need to calculate the difference between the sale price and the original purchase price, also known as the "cost basis."  Your brokerage firm will typically keep track of your cost basis and provide you with an annual report that includes this information. You will use this report to compute the amount of tax owed on your stock sales.  The tax authorities will also receive a copy of this report, and you will need to report the gain or loss on your tax return. If you fail to report the cost basis, the tax authorities may assume it is $0, which could result in a higher tax liability.  It's a good idea to keep records of your stock purchases and sales, including the date, price, and number of shares, in case you need to verify the cost basis or calculate the gain or loss.

The Heath-Jarrow-Morton (HJM) framework is a widely used approach for modeling the term structure of interest rates. It is a general framework that allows for the modeling of the entire yield curve, rather than just a single interest rate.  The HJM framework is based on the idea of modeling the forward rate curve, which is the curve of forward interest rates for different maturities. The forward rate curve is defined as the rate at which a borrower can lock in a loan for a specific period of time, starting at a future date.  The HJM framework models the evolution of the forward rate curve over time using a stochastic process. The framework is based on the following equation:  df(t,T) = μ(t,T)dt + σ(t,T)dW(t)  where:  * f(t,T) is the forward rate at time t for a loan maturing at time T  * μ(t,T) is the drift term, which represents the expected change in the forward rate  * σ(t,T) is the volatility term, which represents the uncertainty in the forward rate  * dW(t) is a Brownian motion, which represents the random shocks to the forward rate  The HJM framework is a very general framework, and it can be difficult to work with in its full generality. To make it more tractable, several simplifying assumptions have been proposed, including:  1. Gaussian HJM: This assumes that the volatility term is constant, and that the drift term is a linear function of the forward rate.  2. Markovian HJM: This assumes that the forward rate curve can be represented as a function of a finite number of state variables, which follow a Markov process.  3. Affine HJM: This assumes that the drift term and volatility term are affine functions of the forward rate.  These simplifying assumptions make it possible to derive closed-form solutions for the prices of interest rate derivatives, such as bonds and options. They also make it possible to estimate the parameters of the model using historical data.

Additionally, 401(k) and IRA contributions may be tax-deductible, reducing your taxable income. However, withdrawals from these accounts are taxed as ordinary income.

It's generally recommended to pay taxes now and invest in a Roth IRA or 401K if you're currently in a lower tax bracket. Forex brokers make money through the bid-ask spread, which is the difference between the buy and sell prices of a currency pair. They typically don't charge commissions because they assume market risk by serving as a counterparty to the investor's trade. Instead, they earn a profit from the spread, which can be fixed or variable. Some brokers may charge a commission based on a percentage of the spread, but this is less common. This business model differs from the stock market, where brokers charge a commission for executing trades on an exchange.

While most forex brokers make their money through the bid-ask spread and don't charge commissions, there are some brokers who do charge a commission, often based on a percentage of the spread or as a fixed fee. However, this is less common than brokers who solely rely on the spread for their revenue.

Stockbrokers make money differently than forex brokers. Stockbrokers typically charge a commission for each trade, which is a fee for executing the trade on behalf of the client. This commission is usually a flat rate or a percentage of the trade value. In contrast, forex brokers primarily make money from the spread, as I mentioned earlier. Stockbrokers act as intermediaries, taking the client's order to an exchange and attempting to execute it, whereas forex brokers act as dealers, assuming market risk and making money from the bid-ask spread.

In addition to the spread, forex brokers can also earn revenue from interest rates. When a client buys a currency with a lower interest rate and sells a currency with a higher interest rate, the broker charges the client the interest rate differential. Conversely, if the client buys a currency with a higher interest rate and sells a currency with a lower interest rate, the broker pays the client the interest rate differential. This is another way forex brokers can generate revenue, aside from the spread.

As a forex trader, it's essential to be aware of both the spread and the swap rate, as they can affect your trading costs and overall profitability. Understanding these costs can help you make more informed trading decisions and manage your risk more effectively.

Flat-rate fees are more commonly associated with stock trading, rather than forex trading. Some stockbrokers charge a flat fee per trade, which can be beneficial for clients who trade in bulk. However, in forex trading, the spread and swap rate are more common ways for brokers to make money.

When buying stocks, a market order and a limit order are two different types of orders that can be used to execute a trade.

A market order is an instruction to buy or sell a stock at the current market price. When a market order is placed, the trade is executed immediately at the best available price. This means that the buyer or seller accepts the current market price, and the trade is completed as soon as possible.

A limit order, on the other hand, is an instruction to buy or sell a stock at a specific price or better. When a limit order is placed, the trade is only executed if the stock reaches the specified price. If the stock does not reach the specified price, the order remains open until it is canceled or expires.

For example, if an investor wants to buy 100 shares of a stock that is currently trading at $50, a market order would execute the trade at $50. However, if the investor places a limit order to buy 100 shares at $45, the trade will only be executed if the stock price falls to $45 or lower.

Limit orders provide more control over the price at which a trade is executed, but they also carry the risk that the trade may not be executed at all if the specified price is not reached. Market orders, on the other hand, ensure that the trade is executed quickly, but the price may not be the best available.

When comparing a fund to an index, a low beta suggests that the fund's returns are less volatile than the index. However, if the R-squared is also low (less than 70), it means that the fund's returns do not closely follow the index's returns. In this case, the low beta loses significance, as the fund's performance is not closely tied to the index. This indicates that the fund's returns are not well-explained by the index's performance, and other factors may be driving the fund's returns. Therefore, a low beta and low R-squared together suggest that the fund's performance is not closely related to the index, and other metrics, such as alpha and Sharpe ratio, should be considered to get a more complete picture of the fund's performance.

The Sharpe Ratio is calculated by subtracting the risk-free rate (such as the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond rate) from the rate of return for a portfolio, and then dividing the result by the standard deviation of the portfolio returns. The formula is:

Sharpe Ratio = (Portfolio Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Standard Deviation of Portfolio Returns

This ratio helps to measure risk-adjusted performance, showing how much better the portfolio performed compared to the risk-free rate, given its volatility.

In portfolio management, Alpha and Beta are metrics derived from linear regression modeling, where a portfolio's return is compared to a standard index (like the S&P 500). 

- Alpha (b) represents the additional return a portfolio generates beyond what is expected based on its market exposure, essentially the "excess return" or the risk-free return. A high alpha is desirable as it indicates the portfolio is performing well without being affected by market volatility.

- Beta (m) represents the multiple of the return, or the portfolio's sensitivity to market movements. A beta of 1 means the portfolio moves in line with the market, while a beta greater than 1 means it is more volatile, and a beta less than 1 means it is less volatile.

In portfolio analysis, R-squared measures how closely a portfolio's returns follow the returns of a benchmark index, such as the S&P 500. It ranges from 0 to 1, with:

* High R-squared (close to 1): The portfolio's returns closely track the index's returns, indicating a strong correlation.
* Low R-squared (close to 0): The portfolio's returns do not follow the index's returns, indicating a weak correlation.

A high R-squared suggests that the portfolio's performance can be largely explained by the performance of the benchmark index, while a low R-squared indicates that the portfolio's returns are more independent of the index.

Beta can be calculated using linear regression analysis, where the portfolio's returns are plotted against the market's returns. The slope of the resulting regression line represents the Beta. Alternatively, you can use the following formula:

Beta = Covariance (portfolio returns, market returns) / Variance (market returns)

In simpler terms, you can also use the "slope" function in Excel or look up the Beta value on financial websites such as Yahoo Finance.

Dollar-cost averaging is an investment strategy that involves investing a fixed amount of money at regular intervals, regardless of the market's performance. This means that you'll buy more shares when the market is low and fewer shares when the market is high.  By doing so, you'll reduce the impact of market volatility on your investments, as you'll be averaging out the cost of your investments over time. This can help you avoid trying to time the market, which can be difficult and often leads to poor investment decisions.  Dollar-cost averaging can also help you develop a disciplined investment habit, as you'll be investing a fixed amount of money at regular intervals. This can help you stay focused on your long-term investment goals and avoid making emotional decisions based on short-term market fluctuations.  For example, if you invest $100 per month in a mutual fund, you'll buy more shares when the market is low and fewer shares when the market is high. Over time, the average cost of your investments will be lower than if you had invested a lump sum of money at one time.  By using dollar-cost averaging, you can reduce your risk and increase your potential returns over the long term.

Rebalancing your portfolio is the process of adjusting the mix of assets in your portfolio to maintain your target asset allocation. This can help you manage risk by ensuring that your portfolio remains aligned with your investment goals and risk tolerance.  Over time, the value of different assets in your portfolio can change, causing your actual asset allocation to drift away from your target allocation. For example, if stocks have performed well and bonds have performed poorly, your portfolio may become overweight in stocks and underweight in bonds.  Rebalancing your portfolio involves selling some of the assets that have performed well and buying more of the assets that have performed poorly. This can help you reduce the risk of your portfolio by maintaining a consistent asset allocation.  For example, if your target allocation is 60% stocks and 40% bonds, and your portfolio has drifted to 70% stocks and 30% bonds, you can rebalance by selling some stocks and buying more bonds. This can help you reduce the risk of your portfolio by reducing your exposure to the stock market.  Rebalancing can also help you take advantage of lower prices for assets that have performed poorly, which can be a good buying opportunity.  It's generally a good idea to rebalance your portfolio on a regular schedule, such as every 6-12 months, to ensure that your portfolio remains aligned with your investment goals and risk tolerance.

The value of a call option can increase for two reasons: the underlying stock price and the level of the VIX index, which measures implied volatility. As the expiry date approaches, the effect of the VIX index on the call option's value diminishes. This is because the vega of a call option, which measures its sensitivity to volatility, decreases as it gets closer to expiry. At maturity, the value of the call option is only dependent on the price of the underlying stock. This means that big jumps in the VIX index will produce smaller increases in the value of the call option as the expiry date approaches.

No, the VIX index is specifically for S&P 500 options and may not accurately reflect the volatility of a specific stock. If you are trading options on a stock other than the S&P 500, the VIX index is less useful. Additionally, if you are trading an option that is not at the money, your implied volatility may be very different from the VIX index. It's recommended to look at the implied volatility specific to the stock you are trading rather than relying on the VIX index.

The VIX index is calculated based on the prices of S&P 500 index options that are expiring in the near term, typically within a few weeks. It measures the implied volatility of the S&P 500 index, which is a gauge of the market's expected volatility over the next 30 days. The VIX is a mathematical aggregate of the implied volatilities of the S&P 500 Index components, and it's often referred to as the "fear index" because it tends to rise when investors are anxious about market conditions. The VIX does not measure actual or historical volatility, but rather the market's expectations of future volatility.

The VIX index measures the expected volatility of the S&P 500 index over the next 30 days, while VIX futures are contracts that allow investors to bet on the future value of the VIX index. VIX futures are cash-settled, meaning that they are settled in cash rather than the underlying asset. They are also based on the value of the VIX index at a specific point in the future, whereas the VIX index itself is a spot measure of volatility. Additionally, VIX futures can have different expiration dates and may not track the VIX index perfectly due to the cost of rolling the futures contracts.

Implied volatility can significantly affect the price of an option. When implied volatility increases, the price of an option also tends to increase, as traders expect larger price movements in the underlying asset. Conversely, when implied volatility decreases, the price of an option tends to decrease. This is because options are more valuable when there is a higher likelihood of large price movements, as they provide a way to hedge against or speculate on those movements.

When an options trader refers to the vega of a call option, they are talking about the rate of change of the option's price with respect to the implied volatility of the underlying asset. In simpler terms, vega measures how much the price of the option changes when the market's expectation of volatility (implied volatility) changes. A higher vega means that the option's price is more sensitive to changes in implied volatility. As the expiry date approaches, the vega of a call option typically decreases, meaning that changes in implied volatility have less impact on the option's price.

Options can be classified into three categories based on their strike price relative to the current market price of the underlying asset:

1. At-the-money (ATM) options: The strike price is equal to the current market price of the underlying asset.
2. In-the-money (ITM) options: The strike price is favorable compared to the current market price. For call options, this means the strike price is below the current market price, and for put options, it means the strike price is above the current market price.
3. Out-of-the-money (OTM) options: The strike price is unfavorable compared to the current market price. For call options, this means the strike price is above the current market price, and for put options, it means the strike price is below the current market price.

These categories affect the option's value, volatility, and likelihood of being exercised.

The potential drawbacks of day trading include: 

1. High risk of financial loss due to lack of knowledge and experience in evaluating stocks and companies.
2. Inadequate access to real-time data, as most data available to individual traders is 15 minutes or more old.
3. Competition with sophisticated and well-funded firms and individuals who have a significant advantage in the market.
4. The potential for significant financial losses if trades do not go as planned, especially if traders are unable to exit trades quickly.
5. The need for a substantial amount of capital to participate in day trading, with some firms requiring a minimum of $25,000 to access their systems.
6. The risk of developing strategies that may work initially but eventually fail, leading to significant losses.
7. The potential for emotional decision-making and impulsive trades, which can exacerbate losses.

Overall, day trading is considered a high-risk activity that requires careful evaluation, significant knowledge, and experience to navigate successfully.

To become successful in day trading, several factors can be helpful. Firstly, having access to very fast data streams is crucial, enabling traders to make quick decisions as trends develop in the markets. Additionally, a deep understanding of how to evaluate stocks and companies, as well as the ability to read financial reports, is essential. It's also important to be aware of the risks involved and to develop strategies that work, although even successful strategies can eventually fail. Furthermore, having a significant amount of capital can be beneficial, as it allows traders to make up for thin margins with a large volume of trades. Finally, being extremely experienced or having a natural eye for reading markets can also contribute to success in day trading.

Using retail brokerage firms for day trading can pose several risks. One major concern is that their web systems may not provide real-time data quickly enough, hindering traders' ability to make timely decisions. This delay, often 15 minutes or more, can be significant in day trading, where small price movements can greatly impact profitability. Furthermore, retail brokerage firms may charge high commission and transaction fees, which can eat into traders' profits. These limitations can put individual traders at a disadvantage compared to more sophisticated and well-funded firms that have access to faster and more reliable data streams.

The robot's gains do not directly come at the expense of your potential profits. The stock market is not a zero-sum game, and multiple parties can make money from the same stock over different time frames.

The stock market makes money on average because companies within it grow in value as the economy grows. Some option trades, specifically those involving selling options without owning the underlying asset, can have limited potential gains and unlimited potential losses. An example is selling a naked call option.

For instance, if you sell a naked call option for $100 with a strike price of $20 for 100 shares, you make money as long as the stock price is under $21. Your potential gain is limited to the $100 you sold the option for. However, if the stock price rises significantly above $20, the buyer of the option can exercise it, and you will be required to sell the stock at the lower strike price, resulting in potentially unlimited losses.

Investing in index funds and buying stocks from the S&P 500 at random differ in terms of risk and volatility. Buying index funds, such as those tracking the S&P 500, allows you to own a diversified portfolio of all the stocks in the index, providing broad market exposure and reduced risk. In contrast, buying individual stocks from the S&P 500 at random can result in a more concentrated and potentially riskier portfolio, as you are selecting a subset of stocks rather than the entire index. While the average return of randomly selected S&P 500 stocks may be similar to that of an index fund, the volatility and risk of the random portfolio will likely be higher.

Selling the market short typically results in losses over time on average because the market as a whole tends to increase in value over time. Historically, the stock market has experienced an average annual growth rate of around 6-10%. When you sell the market short, you are betting against this overall upward trend, expecting the market to decline. However, since the market generally rises over time, the odds are against you, and you are likely to incur losses. Additionally, short selling involves borrowing stocks to sell them, and if the market rises, you will have to buy back the stocks at a higher price to cover your short position, resulting in a loss.

A negative coupon and a negative yield are not the same thing. A negative yield refers to a situation where the investor buys a bond at a price that is higher than the face value of the bond, and the interest payments made by the bond are not enough to offset the loss of principal. This means that the investor will receive less than their initial investment when the bond matures.

A negative coupon, on the other hand, does not exist in the classical sense. However, a bond can have a positive coupon (interest payment) but still have a negative yield. This occurs when the bond is purchased at a premium (above its face value) and the interest payments are not enough to offset the loss of principal. In this case, the investor will receive the coupon payments, but the yield on the bond is still negative because the investor will not get back their full initial investment.

It is not possible for an investor to profit from a bond with a negative coupon in the classical sense. A negative coupon means that the investor is paying more in interest than they are receiving, resulting in a net loss. However, an investor might still buy a bond with a negative coupon if they expect the price of the bond to increase due to changes in market conditions, such as a decrease in interest rates. In this case, the investor could sell the bond at a higher price than they bought it for, resulting in a profit. This profit would not come from the coupon payments, but rather from the capital gain on the sale of the bond.

According to the provided documents, the relationship between corporate tax rates and capital investment is not straightforward. While it is often stated that lowering taxes increases capital investment, this is considered an oversimplification. The actual impact of corporate tax rates on investment depends on the investment rate, which is the rate at which companies invest their profits.

If a company has more money due to lower taxes, it will spend it to maximize profit, not necessarily to grow GDP. In some cases, such as when a company captures a monopoly, this can even be bad for GDP.

Therefore, simply stating that "lowering taxes increases investment" is insufficient. To determine the actual impact, one needs to estimate the investment rate from a marginal reduction in taxes and compare it to the investment rate resulting from a marginal fiscal program spending increase.

When deciding whether to pay off a low-interest loan or invest the money elsewhere, consider the following steps:

1. Evaluate the loan terms: Check if the loan has 0% interest and no penalties for late payments.
2. Assess your financial discipline: Consider your ability to make timely payments and avoid overspending.
3. Weigh the mathematical advantage: Investing the money elsewhere may yield higher returns, but consider the risks involved.
4. Factor in peace of mind: Paying off debt can provide a sense of security and reduce stress.
5. Consider future financial plans: Think about upcoming expenses, job security, and potential need for future borrowing.
6. Calculate the potential risks: Consider the possibility of market crashes or investment losses.
7. Make an informed decision: Balance the mathematical advantage of investing with your personal financial goals and risk tolerance.

Ultimately, there is no one-size-fits-all answer, and the decision depends on individual circumstances and priorities.

The newly discovered planet HD 63433 d is approximately 1.1 times the diameter of Earth, making it very close to Earth's size. However, it is much younger than Earth, at about 400 million years old, compared to Earth's 4.5 billion years. Additionally, HD 63433 d orbits its star at a much closer distance, with a 4.2-day long "year" compared to Earth's 365-day year. Specifically, it is 8 times closer to its star than Mercury is to the Sun, resulting in extremely high temperatures on its dayside, reaching around 2,294 Fahrenheit (1,257 Celsius).

The temperature on the dayside of HD 63433 d can reach approximately 2,294 Fahrenheit (1,257 Celsius), which is comparable to lava worlds like CoRoT-7 b and Kepler-10 b. This extreme heat has led the team behind the discovery to suggest that the planet's dayside could be a "lava hemisphere."
It is likely that HD 63433 d lacks a substantial atmosphere due to its small size, young age, and extremely close proximity to its star.
HD 63433 is a G-type star, which is the same type as our Sun. It is also similar in size to the Sun, being about 0.91 times the size and 0.99 times the mass of the Sun.

The discovery of HD 63433 d was made by a team of astronomers analyzing data from NASA's TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite). They spotted a small object transiting across the star HD 63433, which turned out to be the new planet. To make the discovery, the team removed the signals of two previously known planets in the system from the data, allowing them to see an additional signal - a small transit that reappeared every 4.2 days. Further investigation validated that this signal was indeed a third, smaller planet, HD 63433 d.
The orbital period of HD 63433 d is approximately 4.2 days, which is extremely short compared to Earth's 365-day orbital period.

A "lava hemisphere" refers to the extremely hot dayside of a tidally locked planet, such as HD 63433 d, where temperatures are so high that the surface could be a sea of molten lava. In the case of HD 63433 d, its dayside temperature of around 2,294 Fahrenheit (1,257 Celsius) is comparable to those of known "lava worlds" like CoRoT-7 b and Kepler-10 b.

Galaxies come in various shapes, primarily spirals, ellipticals, and irregulars. 

Spiral galaxies resemble giant rotating pinwheels with a pancake-like disk of stars and a central bulge or tight concentration of stars. Examples include the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy.

Elliptical galaxies have shapes that range from completely round to oval, with little gas and dust, and show very little organization or structure. An example is NGC 2865.

Lenticular galaxies are a cross between spirals and ellipticals, having a central bulge and disk but no arms. An example is NGC 4886.

Irregular galaxies have unusual shapes, like toothpicks, rings, or even little groupings of stars. An example is NGC 5264.

Scientists think that the presence of a bar in spiral galaxies, also known as barred spirals, indicates that they have reached full maturity. However, the provided documents do not specifically explain why scientists think the presence of a bar indicates full maturity.

Active galaxies are galaxies that have centers that appear more than 100 times brighter than the combined light of their stars. This excess energy is thought to come from areas near the galaxies' central supermassive black holes. The black hole's gravity compresses and heats the surrounding gas and dust, causing it to glow across multiple wavelengths, from infrared to X-rays. Active galaxies can be spiral, elliptical, or irregular, and they are characterized by the presence of an accretion disk, a torus, and jets of particles that move near the speed of light. In contrast, inactive galaxies, like the Milky Way, do not have such a high level of activity in their centers and do not emit as much energy. The main difference between active and inactive galaxies is the presence of a strong energy source, likely a supermassive black hole, that is actively accreting material and emitting intense radiation.

In active galaxies, supermassive black holes play a crucial role in producing the excess brightness observed at their centers. The black hole's strong gravity attracts and accretes surrounding gas and dust, forming an accretion disk. As the material in the disk spirals towards the black hole, it becomes compressed and heated, causing it to emit large amounts of energy across multiple wavelengths, from infrared to X-rays. This energy release is responsible for the characteristic brightness of active galaxies. The black hole's mass, which can range from hundreds of thousands to billions of times that of the Sun, determines the amount of energy released, with more massive black holes producing more luminous active galaxies.

Astronomers classify active galaxies based on their distinctive characteristics and behaviors, which are thought to be influenced by the angle at which we view the galaxy's central supermassive black hole and its accretion disk.  During the early 20th century, astronomers began classifying active galaxies based on their observed properties. They now believe that many of the signature traits of active galaxies are a result of viewing the centers of these galaxies at different angles, such as seeing directly into the torus versus seeing it from the side.  Active galaxies can also be categorized by their brightness in radio wavelengths. This classification system helps astronomers understand the diverse range of active galaxy behaviors and the underlying physical processes that drive their activity.

The HEASARC archive and LAMBDA archive were separate archives that merged in 2008. Prior to the merger, the main difference between the two archives was the focus of their data collections. The HEASARC archive focused on high-energy astronomy missions observing in the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV), X-ray, and gamma-ray bands. In contrast, the LAMBDA archive focused on data from space missions, balloons, and ground-based facilities that studied the relic cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation in the sub-mm, mm, and cm bands. After the merger, the HEASARC archive now contains data from both high-energy astronomy missions and CMB radiation research.

The Swift XRT CALDB and NuSTAR FPM caldb are both calibration databases for X-ray space missions. The main difference between them is that they are used for different space missions and instruments.

The Swift XRT CALDB is used for the X-Ray Telescope (XRT) instrument on the Swift space mission. Swift is a NASA mission that was launched in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts and other high-energy astrophysical phenomena. The XRT is one of the instruments on board Swift, and it is used to observe X-rays emitted by these phenomena.

The NuSTAR FPM caldb, on the other hand, is used for the Focal Plane Module (FPM) instrument on the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) space mission. NuSTAR is a NASA mission that was launched in 2012 to study high-energy X-rays emitted by black holes, neutron stars, and other astrophysical sources. The FPM is one of the instruments on board NuSTAR, and it is used to focus and detect X-rays.

In terms of the updates mentioned in the text, the Swift XRT CALDB was updated to version 20240522 to update the XRT gains, while the NuSTAR FPM caldb was updated to version 20240520 to include a new clock correction file (v183). These updates are likely intended to improve the accuracy and reliability of the data collected by these instruments.

This integration enables seamless access to HEASARC's data and resources within the broader Virtual Observatory framework, facilitating data discovery, analysis, and sharing across different astronomical archives and communities.

Additionally, users can also access the HEASARC's VO-enabled services through other VO-compatible tools and interfaces, such as those provided by the International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA) and the NASA Astronomical Virtual Observatories (NAVO).

The California Air Resources Board (CARB) is the primary state agency responsible for protecting public health from the harmful effects of air pollution. Its key responsibilities include:

1. Leading California's efforts to reduce climate-changing emissions and promoting a more energy-efficient and resilient economy.
2. Setting the state's air quality standards to protect those at greatest risk, such as children, older adults, and people with lung and heart disease.
3. Identifying pollutants that pose the greatest health risks and measuring progress in reducing pollutants using the nation's most extensive air monitoring network.
4. Verifying automakers' emissions compliance and researching the causes and effects of air pollution problems.
5. Studying the costs and benefits of pollution controls, with a focus on individuals and communities most at risk.

CARB also works to address air pollution in heavily urbanized communities and those adjacent to busy freight corridors, and has established programs to address pollution in these areas. Additionally, CARB has pioneered many approaches to address air quality problems, including guiding the activities of 35 local air pollution control districts and leading the state's efforts to address global climate change.

2. CARB, which focuses on California's unique air quality challenges by setting the state's own stricter emissions standards for a range of statewide pollution sources, including vehicles, fuels, and consumer products.
3. Thirty-five local air pollution control districts, which regulate emissions from businesses and stationary facilities, ranging from oil refineries to auto body shops and dry cleaners.

This coordinated approach allows CARB to work with other organizations to effectively address air pollution in California.

According to the documents, potential signs of life on exoplanets like Gliese 12 b could include the presence of certain gases in the atmosphere, such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and methane, which could be detected by telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope. Additionally, signs of photosynthesis or the presence of animal life could also be detected. However, it is essential to note that these signs do not necessarily confirm the presence of life but rather provide an estimate of probability. In the case of Gliese 12 b, studying its atmosphere could help determine its habitability and provide insights into the evolution of our own solar system.

Gliese 12 b, being between Earth and Venus in temperature, could teach us about the habitability pathways planets take as they develop. Its atmosphere could provide insights into how planets retain or lose their atmospheres, and how this affects their habitability. Specifically, studying Gliese 12 b may help scientists understand why Earth is habitable while Venus is not, despite both planets having similar initial conditions. This knowledge can shed light on the evolutionary processes that shape the habitability of planets across the galaxy.

The storminess of Gliese 12, the host star, is significant in the habitability of Gliese 12 b because red dwarfs like Gliese 12 tend to be magnetically active, resulting in frequent, powerful X-ray flares. However, analyses have concluded that Gliese 12 shows no signs of extreme behavior, which could be beneficial for the habitability of Gliese 12 b, as a calm star is less likely to strip away the planet's atmosphere.

The James Webb Space Telescope can help in studying Gliese 12 b by analyzing the light that passes through the planet's atmosphere during a transit. This can provide a set of chemical fingerprints that can be detected by the telescope, allowing scientists to determine the composition of the atmosphere and whether it retains an atmosphere. This information can help scientists better understand the habitability of Gliese 12 b.

The estimated size of Gliese 12 b is comparable to that of Earth or slightly smaller, similar to Venus. Assuming it has no atmosphere, the planet's surface temperature is estimated to be around 107 degrees Fahrenheit (42 degrees Celsius).

The advantages of looking for habitable planets around red dwarf stars include:

1. Easier detection: The smaller size and mass of red dwarf stars make it easier to detect Earth-size planets, as the dimming effect of a transit is greater and the wobble of the star (reflex motion) is more pronounced.
2. Closer habitable zones: The lower luminosity of red dwarf stars means that their habitable zones are closer to the star, making it easier to detect transiting planets within these zones.

Gliese 12 b's ability to retain its atmosphere and be habitable despite its close proximity to its star is uncertain. However, the fact that its host star, Gliese 12, shows no signs of extreme behavior, such as frequent and powerful X-ray flares, suggests that the planet's atmosphere might be stable. Further study, such as with the James Webb Space Telescope, is needed to determine if Gliese 12 b can retain its atmosphere and potentially be habitable.
